title: Can Banks Seize The Revenue Opportunity As Gen AI Costs Decline?
text:
Much has been written about whether generative AI will conform with the familiar technology hype cycle, and if so, whether the Trough of Disillusionment awaits. Fueling much of this debate is the current high cost of deploying, training and using the technology.
I believe there are two factors that aren’t receiving enough attention in this discussion: credible projections of a sharp decline in cost, and the likely impact of generative AI on banks’ revenue.
Starting with cost, potential users of the technology stand to benefit greatly from a combinatorial effect caused by three powerful forces. The first is a rapid decline in the cost of compute. Many have predicted the weakening, if not the demise, of Moore’s Law, which says the number of transistors on a computer chip – and therefore its output – doubles every two years at roughly the same cost. And yet Nvidia’s graphics processing units, which power many generative AI models, have increased their computational power by more than a thousand times over the past eight years.
Amplifying this rapid expansion in hardware productivity is a dramatic improvement in the software – the algorithms that account for the magic of generative AI. We’re also seeing a proliferation of more economical midsize and small language models, which require less training and less compute.
And then the third force that is helping drive down cost is captured by Wright’s Law, which says that as we work on and use a new product, our improved skills and processes reduce costs by a fixed proportion each year. Major banks like JPMorganChase, which recently launched a suite of generative AI tools to help more than 50,000 of its employees work more efficiently, are likely to gain an early advantage from this move.
What about the revenue?
The second factor which I believe deserves more attention is the potential of generative AI not only to increase productivity but also, and more importantly, drive revenue. Lately, a number of commentators have questioned whether businesses can actually do this or if the technology will end up being only an efficiency play. Most of the industry refutes this – Accenture’s Pulse of Change survey, published in June, found that 76% of banking executives globally view generative AI as more beneficial to revenue growth than to cost reduction.
To me, the reason we aren’t yet seeing the revenue lift is simple: banks have literally hundreds of use case ideas, but are prioritizing against the capabilities that are actually out there today at the right price point. As is often the case with new technologies, there is also an initial preference for applications that build confidence by generating quick returns – and cost plays tend to beat revenue generation when rapid ROI is the goal.
A good example is call centers. I don’t know of a single bank that isn’t using generative AI to help its reps do their post-call summaries. It’s an early and quite basic use case that requires limited compute, but it can save 15-20% of the reps’ call time so it’s a no-brainer. At the other end of the spectrum, a few financial institutions are thinking about taking all their data on all their customer interactions and using it to build a digital brain that will enable their call center to become a powerful channel for personalized sales outreach. This more complex use case will take longer to realize, but it has the potential to be a game changer for the industry.
Why now, if it will be cheaper tomorrow?
All of this creates the dilemma that’s familiar to anyone thinking of investing in new technology: why invest now if it will cost less in the future?
The answer lies in the reasoning of everyone who has bought a new-generation smartphone soon after its release: the immediate benefits matter more than the saving that can be realized by waiting. The fact that generative AI is being investigated, piloted and adopted at such an incredible pace confirms that the expected benefits matter greatly. There is also recognition that it will provide early adopters with a competitive advantage that will take the more hesitant firms time and effort to overcome.
In light of this, there are three things I’d recommend banks do at the moment:
1. Act decisively, but prudently. You know that prioritizing potential use cases, training your people to use generative AI, and fostering a culture that embraces learning and new ways of working can’t be done overnight – so the sooner you get started, the sooner you’ll be ready.
2. Lay out your horizons. Identify where and how you want to use generative AI over time. Then figure out the data, talent and technology you will need to realize that ambition and develop a plan of attack that takes all factors into account. You don’t want to be building use cases for the BlackBerry when the iPhone is coming.
3. Ride the deflationary cost curve. Ensure that your plan takes advantage of falling costs, but bear in mind that waiting too long could be a false economy that will cost you in unexpected ways. Keep your plan flexible. In some cases, it may benefit you to switch from one model to another, to adjust or upgrade, or to shuffle your priorities as the technology gets better and cheaper.
On the brink of transformation
Right now, banks are sitting in a similar position to where they were in 2005: structured and equipped for a marketplace reliant on online banking over PCs and laptops, but aware that the iPhone was coming and with it the mobile app. Everyone sensed that banking was about to be transformed.
That’s where we are today with generative AI. Is it evolution or revolution? Will it simply cut costs or enable entirely new business and operating models for banking? It’s important not to get lost in the debate, much of which is based on different technologies in earlier times. That’s a bit like driving 200 mph and trying to steer by keeping an eye on the rear-view mirror.
Generative AI has a lot in common with earlier technologies, but it’s exciting because it’s also very different, and hard to predict. Most bankers believe it has the potential to transform not only their businesses but also the industry. So my advice is: make your plans and do your sums carefully, but allow yourself to get a little excited about this once-in-a-lifetime innovation.

title: Council Post: AI Is Asking A Lot Of Our Data—How Can We Humans Help It Out?
text:
Adrian Carr is CEO of global master data management solution provider Stibo Systems, which empowers companies through data transparency.
Where we stand now, AI is a siren promising to revolutionize anything and everything we experience. Its impact is poignantly felt within the business sphere, making waves all the way from backend data analysis to customer interactions. It might even make you wonder if your company needs to exist in the future. But let’s not get ahead of ourselves—we're still years away from becoming totally irrelevant.
As AI works tirelessly to carve its place in this world, we can't forget the irreplaceable role of human oversight. Although AI tools can churn out data and streamline processes at mind-numbing speeds, it's the human-in-the-loop that gives content depth, authenticity and that magic spark. It’s tricky to put a finger on, but you know it when you see it—and when you don’t.
Artificial intelligence (AI) was created by humans to make human lives easier. So, how can we help AI better serve us?
Data As A Differentiator
By now, it's not up for debate that AI can handle vast amounts of data and make processes more efficient. Businesses know it, their stakeholders know it and their customers know it. A PYMNTS study found that "78% of business leaders rank generative AI as the most impactful emerging technology over the next three to five years."
Investments on every level are going to have to be made to compete, especially when it comes to a business’ technology stack. As International Data Corporation’s Rick Villars puts it, "Every IT provider will incorporate AI into the core of their business, investing treasure, brainpower, and time."
The ability to gather and leverage accurate and credible data—and avoid misinformation—is a critical competitive differentiator. As new technologies arrive onto the scene, requiring the ability to rapidly pull and produce content from every source available, data you can trust becomes more and more essential.
Feed AI With Data You Can Bank On
It’s common sense that organizations can promote data reliability by establishing a single source of truth for all that organization’s information. Looking ahead, trustworthy data continues to be essential for businesses seeking to leverage AI technologies effectively. Maintaining a golden record of information—from customer to location to sustainability data—can be a foundation for making informed decisions and navigating complexities with confidence, even with decreased human intervention.
Master data management (MDM) should play a pivotal role in an organization’s AI strategy both today and tomorrow. There's a symbiotic relationship between AI and MDM in enhancing operational efficiency and streamlining complex processes (such as data integration, cleansing and governance), freeing up time for human employees and empowering them to focus on other meaningful tasks. How much companies are willing to invest in their data management strategies will have a direct impact on their ability to navigate this dynamic era effectively.
Data Privacy And Ethics
As we integrate AI deeper into our business processes, it's also crucial to address data privacy and ethical considerations. Although this topic could be an article unto itself, it must be pointed out that regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in Europe and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) in the U.S. have set stringent standards for data protection and user privacy.
Companies must ensure that their AI systems comply with these regulations to maintain customer trust and avoid potentially devastating legal repercussions. Adopting ethical AI frameworks, such as those proposed by the IEEE or the European Commission, can guide organizations in developing transparent and fair AI solutions. With the cloud of generalized uncertainty around AI, we must do what we can to foster a culture of responsibility and trust to keep customer loyalty.
Working Together
AI may still fall short when it comes to understanding the subtleties of human emotions and language. Humans are still the ones who can transform raw data into compelling content that resonates—something AI has yet to master. But we know it’s going to get there, and when it does, our technology stacks must be ready to meet it.
As AI becomes an even bigger part of our lives and businesses, let's remember to anchor our strategies in data we can truly trust. AI and machine learning are incredible tools, but it's the combination of AI’s efficiency and human involvement that will drive innovation forward. We can do our part by feeding AI with the pipelines of accurate data it needs to serve us in a way we won’t regret.

title: Council Post: Sustainable Aviation: Navigating The Fourth Revolution In Aerospace
text:
Greg Ombach, Head of Disruptive Research & Technology, Senior Vice President at Airbus.
The aerospace industry is undergoing one of the most significant changes in history. This change is driven by the urgent need for sustainability, specifically focusing on reaching net-zero carbon emissions by 2050. This ambitious target responds to the environmental impact of aviation, which contributes around 2.5% of global carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions. As the industry looks to the future, it is exploring various technologies and innovations to reduce its carbon footprint. Aviation is now entering its fourth major revolution. The first revolution made planes fly, the second focused on safety and the third democratized air travel, making it accessible globally.
Today, the fourth revolution centers on sustainability, representing a fundamental change in how the aerospace industry operates. In addition to CO2 emissions, the sector is tackling contrails—white streaks left by aircraft that contribute to global warming by trapping heat in the atmosphere. Addressing contrails is essential to minimizing aviation's environmental impact.
The Net-Zero Challenge
Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 is a complex challenge. Aviation currently emits approximately 445 million tons of CO2 annually, a small but significant portion of the 37.4 billion tons of global CO2 emissions. Over the past three decades, the industry has reduced emissions by 50%. However, achieving the subsequent 50% reduction will require drastic measures and innovations, mainly as air travel demand grows and is expected to double by 2040.
Technological Innovations For Sustainability
One of the most promising avenues for reducing emissions is through advancements in aircraft technology. Modern aircraft are already 20% more fuel-efficient than their predecessors, thanks to improvements in aerodynamics, engine performance and the use of lighter materials. These advancements are critical as the industry seeks to reduce fuel consumption and emissions further.
New wing designs are being explored, using longer, leaner and lighter wings that optimize aerodynamics. These wings may feature intelligent surfaces that adjust in real-time to flight conditions, enhancing performance. In parallel, hybrid propulsion systems are being developed, combining traditional jet engines with electric power to reduce emissions and noise.
The Promise Of Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF)
Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF) are being developed alongside these innovations to replace conventional jet fuel. SAFs have the potential to reduce lifecycle CO2 emissions by up to 80%, making them a crucial part of the industry's strategy to lower its carbon footprint. Achieving this goal requires mobilizing the entire supply chain to ensure sufficient production at competitive costs, involving scaling up production, improving logistics and collaborating with stakeholders to create a viable SAF market.
Hydrogen-Powered Aircraft: The Next Frontier
Hydrogen-powered aircraft offer a zero-emission alternative to traditional fuels. By 2035, the first commercial hydrogen-powered aircraft are expected to enter service, utilizing hydrogen either as fuel for direct combustion or for generating electricity via fuel cells. Developing hydrogen infrastructure, including storage and refueling systems, will be crucial for the widespread adoption of this technology.
AI Strategy In Aerospace
The integration of AI into the aerospace industry is broad and focuses on key areas that drive both efficiency and innovation. AI streamlines routine tasks like email management and knowledge systems, freeing employees to focus on strategic initiatives. In operations, AI enhances resource management and customer service by predicting maintenance needs and optimizing service delivery, leading to more reliable processes. Moreover, AI is crucial in designing safer, more efficient aircraft by simulating scenarios and analyzing extensive data sets, helping engineers create reliable products. Additionally, AI-driven tools assist airlines in optimizing operations, making air travel more efficient and enhancing the customer experience.
The Role of AI And Big Data
Artificial intelligence and big data are increasingly pivotal in helping the aerospace industry meet its sustainability goals. AI optimizes various aspects of aircraft operations, from enhancing fuel efficiency to improving safety. Modern aircraft, such as the Airbus A350, generate vast amounts of data—up to 2.5 terabytes per day. This data is analyzed to predict maintenance needs, optimize flight paths and enhance overall operational efficiency. Predictive maintenance, powered by AI, reduces the need for unscheduled maintenance by identifying potential failures before they occur.
AI can also drive innovative concepts like formation flight, which takes inspiration from the V-formation of migrating birds. This approach, as demonstrated in projects like Fello'fly, reduces air resistance and saves fuel by having aircraft fly in close formation.
Future Opportunities
Several future opportunities are poised to revolutionize the aerospace industry’s approach to sustainability. Sustainable supply chain optimization, driven by AI, will be crucial in reducing carbon footprints by improving logistics and resource management efficiency. Smart automation and enhanced autonomous flight capabilities are also on the horizon, with projects pioneering autonomous flight systems to improve safety and operational efficiency.
The continued development of hybrid propulsion systems offers the potential for quieter, more fuel-efficient flights. Future advancements in materials science will create lighter, stronger and more sustainable materials, helping reduce fuel consumption and emissions.
Overcoming Challenges
While the potential of AI and big data in transforming the aerospace industry is immense, there are still significant challenges that must be addressed. Ensuring the trustworthiness and safety of AI systems, standardizing and regulating new technologies and maintaining sovereignty in AI development are critical hurdles. The industry must foster collaboration between AI experts, engineers, regulators and other stakeholders to drive innovation while ensuring safety and compliance. Additionally, deploying these technologies will require substantial investment and global cooperation.
The success of initiatives like hydrogen propulsion and SAF depends on technological advancements and the development of supporting infrastructure and regulatory frameworks.
Conclusion
The journey to net-zero aviation by 2050 is ambitious but achievable. The aerospace industry is making significant strides toward reducing its environmental impact by integrating AI, big data and innovative technologies.
This fourth revolution is not just about meeting regulatory requirements or reducing costs—it’s about ensuring that the aviation industry can continue to connect people and cultures worldwide without compromising our planet's health.

title: Making Enterprises Resilient In The Face Of Growing Cyber Threats
text:
The cost of global cybercrime has surpassed $10 trillion, reflecting the relentless growth in the scale and scope of data breaches, ransomware attacks and malicious disruption to business and government operations. “There is no doubt that the number, the quantity, and the quality of cyber attacks are rising,” says Ram Elboim, CEO of Sygnia, provider of cyber readiness and response services to enterprises worldwide.
Elboim reports that “geopolitics play today a much larger role in cybersecurity than in the past.” Enterprises now experience attacks from what’s for them is a completely new corner of the cyber landscape—nation-state threat actors. Members of these cyber armies are especially successful in attacking new targets, including organizations that support critical infrastructure such as power plants and water supply systems or that provide vital services such as hospitals.
Another relatively new dimension to the rise in cyber attacks is a focus on disrupting and damaging a supply chain, says Elboim. This could be an attack on the specific sequence of connections used by a commercial supplier or infiltrating a piece of software, including cybersecurity software, used by many enterprises. Because of the increased use of open-source software libraries, there was a 28% annual increase in 2023 in the total number of malicious packages uploaded to open-source repositories.
Another growing segment of this growth industry is ransomware, with ransomware payments in the U.S. in the first half of 2024 reaching nearly $460 million. “Ransomware now is a very big business and it is run as a business,” says Elboim.
In addition to the growing sophistication of cyber criminals, two important components of today’s business operations are contributing to the significant expansion in the scale and scope of cyber threat. One is legacy IT infrastructure that hasn’t been updated to protect it from new types of threats. For example, says Elboim, a machine controlling an assembly line. The factory management is reluctant to arm it with new cybersecurity tools because that entails the costly step of shutting down the assembly line. Today, attackers are looking for such vulnerabilities.
The other factor contributing to the increase in the number of cyber attacks is the growing incorporation of all types of enterprises in the relatively new IT infrastructure of the cloud and the global network of the internet. Hospitals, for example, used to be quite isolated and insulated, but not anymore. In the first half of this year, 387 data breaches of 500 or more records were reported by U.S. hospitals, an 8.4% increase from the first half of 2023, and a 9.3% increase from the first half of 2022.
Joining the new, global IT infrastructure also means having to keep up with its never-ending transformations and constant upgrading with new technologies, applications and services. Today, the new new thing is AI with McKinsey reporting earlier this year that AI adoption by enterprises worldwide has jumped to 72% percent. A new GlobalData report summarizing Q2 2024 company filings found widespread discussion of the need to implement tools and processes to mitigate increased cybersecurity risks. Companies experimenting with new applications of AI have realized that integrating it with existing infrastructure and operations creates a growing attack surface that demands greater scrutiny.
“There is a lot of promise in AI in terms of improving cybersecurity tools,” says Elboim. But AI also potentially increases cyber risks, as many enterprises haven’t yet established clear governance rules around AI and don’t have an accurate accounting of how AI is being used by their employees. “This opens a new threat landscape for organizations,” says Elboim. Sygnia and NVIDIA recently announced a hardware and software solution intended to secure industrial and critical infrastructure with AI-powered security at the edge.
Sygnia employs about 250 professionals, based in offices in Tel Aviv, New York, Singapore, London, Mexico City and Sydney. They provide consulting and assistance to enterprises in terms of preventing and defending from cyber attacks; response, remediation and recovery from cyber attacks; and monitoring and detection of cyber threats. Founded in 2015 by veterans of Israel’s elite intelligence group Unit 8200, Sygnia was launched by the Team8 startup foundry, also established by 8200 alumni. Initially funded by Microsoft, Intel, Cisco, Qualcomm, AT&T, Nokia, Temasek and Innovation Endeavors, Sygnia became a Temasek International company in 2018.
Noting that venture investment has fallen by about half from its peak in 2022, the Wall Street Journal recently highlighted cybersecurity as a sector still getting fresh funding, and the significant role Israeli cybersecurity startups—and 8200 alumni—play in attracting private and public investors: “Members of Unit 8200, known for its advanced cybersecurity and cyberwarfare capabilities, have founded dozens of cybersecurity companies. Others have become influential venture capitalists in their own rights and are mentors to entrepreneurial graduates.”
The expertise Israelis have gained in cyber warfare has contributed to the creation of a successful cybersecurity industry ($2.8 billion-worth of startup acquisitions in 2023) and defending the country which has encountered 2.5 times more cyber attacks than usual during the current war with Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran. Summing up his many years in the cybersecurity business, including his work as an 8200 officer for which he received Israel’s Defense Prize, Elboim says that “resilience is not necessarily prevention of an attack but being ready when an attack occurs.”

title: Council Post: The Future Of Public Safety: Enhancing Security Through Video Behavior Analytics
text:
Nick Herbert is the Global Head of Government & Public Safety for Fujitsu, enabling a trusted digital society.
I spend much of my working life focused on improving public safety and security for governments, organizations and individuals. As expected, the interest and investment in technology to improve society's safety is increasing daily. Video behavior analytics (VBA), powered by artificial intelligence (AI), is a leading tool in this transformation. It has such potential for good that I believe we all have a responsibility to share our knowledge to strive towards a better, safer society for all.
VBA works by detecting and interpreting human behavior and intent from video streams, transforming safety measures across various industries, from transportation and retail to government facilities, but many are not yet on this journey.
Understanding Video Behavior Analytics
Video behavior analytics involves the use of AI algorithms to analyze video footage and identify humans and their actions to recognize patterns that may indicate suspicious or dangerous behavior. Unlike traditional video surveillance, which relies heavily on human monitoring, VBA automates the detection process, allowing for real-time alerts and quicker responses to potential threats, ideally preventing security incidents before harm is caused. This technology can detect a wide range of behaviors, from aggressive actions and vandalism to individuals entering prohibited areas or showing signs of distress requiring medical assistance.
In 2021, 48,830 people in the U.S. died of gun-related injuries, and 22 million Europeans were physically attacked. Thousands of people are hurt on train lines per year, with 8,000 people in India in 2020 as a key example. Could early video detection of activity reduce this number?
The Impact On Public Safety
The implementation of VBA in public safety is multifaceted, addressing several key areas:
Transportation
One key area is increasing the safety of passengers and drivers by identifying aggressive behavior, vandalism or unauthorized access to restricted areas, such as train tracks. By detecting these behaviors early, transport control centers and station staff can take preventive measures or respond to incidents, minimizing risks and enhancing overall safety.
Government Facilities
Ensuring the safety of citizens within government facilities is critical. VBA can detect threats of suspicious behavior or unauthorized access to sensitive areas, allowing security personnel to step in before incidents escalate.
Educational Institutions
Violence in schools has been well publicized, especially in the United States. Campus safety could be improved with VBA by identifying potential threats, such as unauthorized intrusions, aggression or potential bullying. This use case helps to promote a safer learning environment for students and faculty staff.
Public Events
Large gatherings in public spaces or arenas, such as concerts, sports events and festivals, create unique security challenges. VBA could help monitor crowds for signs of aggression and identify individuals entering restricted areas, left luggage or potential overcrowding.
The Technical Challenge
Many real-world applications of detecting human behavior encounter environmental conditions, which necessitate a flexible approach. A "simple" single-model approach often struggles with precision and recall, especially when dealing with occlusion, where an object or person is partially obscured. Additional issues, such as poor lighting or differences in behavior between "attendees" and "staff in uniforms," call for a more nuanced solution.
By integrating multiple AI models into a multi-modal approach, it is possible to significantly enhance results. For instance, large language models (LLMs) designed for image and video recognition can complement skeletal models used for AI human behavior detection, which can be complemented again by tracking models that can "follow" a person through multiple camera feeds.
The combined approach not only helps improve the overall accuracy but also ensures more robust handling of challenging scenarios, such as poor lighting conditions or crowded environments. Putting tech aside, the aim here is to have a solution that delivers high precision and recall. This ensures that businesses and public sector organizations can deploy more effective systems and trust that the alerts generated indicate situations where action is necessary to enhance safety and security measures.
The Broader Implications For Society
The initial focus on building a business case for vision AI in public safety is often the reduction of operational costs. However, for me, the biggest benefit is in the way that this technology can impact the individual—staff, customers and citizens. By reducing the burden on frontline workers and improving response times, VBA can contribute to being a cornerstone in our public safety infrastructure fabric.
Automating routine tasks can help to reduce stress and mental health issues among employees, allowing them to focus on critical events and alerts. In sectors facing labor shortages, like retail and transportation, VBA boosts workforce productivity, maintaining safety and security and alleviating the burden on frontline workers. Additionally, optimizing monitoring processes can reduce costs by up to 30%, making it a vital component of public safety infrastructure.
Video behavior analytics lays the foundations for a significant step forward in how we improve public safety as a society. Yet, there are privacy concerns and ethical considerations for implementing any computer vision solution within a public domain.
These concerns relate to the installation of video behavior analytics in open public areas, which will trigger privacy and ethical questions. Surveillance inherently implies that people are being watched continually, and though it may be legal, it can be invasive to an individual and without explicit consent. Additionally, there is the threat that such large volumes of data collected could be exploited, whether by external actors or by repurposing the data into other unrelated initiatives. The other often-cited issue is bias. Any AI system has the potential to lead toward bias, only exacerbating existing prejudices and providing unfair outcomes for some groups or communities.
To overcome these obstacles, organizations must adopt a proactive and transparent approach. Explainable AI, with transparent policies and rules, is essential to build trust. It is also important not to forget the value of the "human in the loop." This means that even though AI is used to recommend actions, the final decisions belong to humans—especially when it comes to public safety, security or other sensitive arenas.
For organizations seeking to implement this type of solution, the importance of outside opinion, stakeholder engagement and community outreach will be a key pillar of your adoption program. No system is perfect, and compromises are often needed. What better way to agree on the priority areas than with the citizens that you seek to serve?
In Summary
By creating an open dialogue and sharing approaches to challenges and successes, we can collaborate between the public and private sectors to advance our application and understanding of the ethical applications of this technology to harness the potential and create a safer, more secure world for all.

title: Bitcoin Intersects With Today’s Most Pivotal Macro Investment Trends
text:
On its’s own, bitcoin is having a stellar year, gaining broader adoption and greater influence. Bitcoin the asset (BTC) is up over 125% in the last 12-months and over 33% year-to-date. BTC spot ETFs, introduced in January 2024, have far exceeded the industry’s performance expectations to become the most successful ETF launch in US history. The group’s Day 1 net flow totalled $655 million on $4.66 billion of trading volume and over $50 billion in AUM has been accumulated across issuers to date. The most technologically sophisticated issuers have already adopted a proof of reserve standard - a capability native to bitcoin - to automatically, in real time, provide public verification of BTC holdings.
Further, bitcoin’s payment network, Lightning Network, has seen strong, organic growth driven by the software’s utility, rather than the token incentives and cryptocurrency speculation that underly most of the engagement in non-bitcoin and non-stablecoin crypto ecosystems. Instead, Lightning Network transactions increased 1,212% over a 24-month period ending in late 2023 as use of the network increased including for cross-border and micropayments, both which Lightning makes more efficient.
From a 10,000 foot view, bitcoin has advanced as a store of value, matured and gained market share as a means of exchange, and increased dominance vs. the crypto market as classic crypto and stablecoin functions and activities have begun moving to bitcoin as they mature. This may be most evident with the flourishment of ZK rollups on bitcoin beginning in 2023.
But bitcoin doesn’t exist in a silo, it emerged in the late 2010s from a two+ prior decades of research and development and today bears significance to other nationally critical industries and large macro investment trends. In July, at the Bitcoin Conference 2024, I joined Cathie Wood, founder CEO and CIO of ARK Invest, to discuss bitcoin’s convergence with the macro investment trends of importance to large asset managers, specifically (I) generative AI and LLM technologies and infrastructure and (II) the energy transition to renewable generation.
First, to reach and capture the full potential in generative AI technologies, investors must consider the payments infrastructure that is fit to serve a field of new capabilities that will likely come to include, for example, per-API call monetization, reliance on multiple models to achieve a solution, AI models that reference (and need to make payment to) other models or external data pools, AI-supported agents that interact and/or transact with an audience (e.g. to issue rewards or incentives) or on behalf of an individual or enterprise (e.g. to filter spam), or more simply, paywalled content and data materials. A mature AI and LLM ecosystem will require cost efficient micropayments on a highly scalable payments architecture, which falls outside of the strengths of traditional financial systems and beyond the system constraints of non-bitcoin cryptocurrencies and their payment focused L2s (“layer twos”).
Uniquely, with bitcoin’s Lightning Network, real time payments are able to match the flow of value in a system. Lightning payments settle instantly and nearly for free, unlocking the potential for efficient microtransactions and opening global access to software and data, including AI models, data pools, and agents or bots.
Within the bitcoin and crypto industries, only bitcoin’s Lightning Network can reach the scale of payments that AI, LLMs, and the agents and bots that will leverage them are expected to achieve. This is because the Lightning Network is a payments channel network and, as such, Lightning payments do not require a global state of network transactions to assure honest transactions. Consequently, Lightning payments do not require the scarce and costly block space of the underlying blockchain outside of specific, anomalous, circumstances. Other blockchain scaling solutions, including ZK rollups, which may have great value for more complex financial contracting on bitcoin, require compute and block space that ultimately caps the number of transactions that may be processed per second. Lightning exists outside of this constraint, enabling it to be a favorable payments partner to the AI field, itself projected to reach $1.3 trillion over the next 10 years according to reporting by Bloomberg Intelligence.
Further, the friction in establishing a payment channel network (a tradeoff to its potential for AI-level scale) is a competitive moat that advantages bitcoin’s Lightning Network against crypto latecomers. Establishing a payment channel network of sufficient scale to offer utility to early adopters requires a bootstrapping period in which a growing number of individuals run nodes (i.e., channel hubs) and contribute capital for network liquidity without receiving much reward in return. Such a network is difficult to establish and to maintain. For example, ethereum's attempt at a payment channel network, Raiden Network, failed- discontinuing development.
In addition to bitcoin’s intersection with AI, bitcoin may drive investor returns and project productivity in the energy transition, where global investment hit $1.8 trillion in 2023, according to BloombergNEF reporting. This figure includes investment in the construction of renewable energy production facilities, such as wind, solar and geothermal power plants, biofuels production plants, and the power grid. Key renewable energy sources, however, suffer from intermittency. Energy supply and demand are frequently mismatched, resulting in significantly more power than is needed during certain recurring periods as well as not enough when demand spikes, and grid congestion exacerbates this. But bitcoin data centers’ large, flexible loads can support power generation assets managing congestion, curtailment, and negative pricing.
Both bitcoin and AI data centers will consume surplus energy, but bitcoin data centers (also known as bitcoin mining facilities) can be significantly more responsive to energy price, which itself reflects the dynamic relationship between supply and demand. Thus, bitcoin data centers don’t contribute to demand peaks as AI data centers do. Because bitcoin miners can fill demand troughs without adding to the peaks, bitcoin mining can improve the return productivity of new renewable energy development. For energy producers with existing, surplus production, bitcoin mining can absorb and monetizes this energy.
Additionally, within the energy field, bitcoin payments technology can reduce credit exposure between energy market stakeholders. Supply and demand on the power grid must match in real time, but payments don’t flow for days or weeks. This leads market operators and energy suppliers to require collateral from buyers to mitigate default risk. Because bitcoin’s Lightning Network enables real time payment, it can reduce credit exposure between such counterparties, freeing billions of dollars of working capital to be used for further development of energy infrastructure.
Energy innovators and generative AI pioneers are blazing the trail for the electric grid to become more sustainable and AI to contribute to greater economic productivity. Both may leverage bitcoin to further the potential of these visions, accelerate their achievement, and support investment productivity.

title: Connection BrandVoice: How Early Movers Are Realizing AI’s Promise
text:
AI has enormous potential to transform businesses, organizations, the work of individuals, and even the habits of consumers. The McKinsey Global Institute estimates that generative AI (GenAI) alone could add $4.4 trillion to annual corporate profits.¹
Yet, following initial excitement around GenAI, some are unsure how to deploy and use it effectively. More than three-quarters of workers (78%) recently surveyed about AI’s impact in the workplace feel positively about AI. However, a majority (61%) also expressed worries that AI would increase rather than reduce their workloads as they adjust to new tools and employer expectations.²
On the organizational side, most business and technology leaders (55%) surveyed about their readiness to deploy AI say their company’s infrastructure lacks the scalability and security it needs to meet AI’s increased demands on data access, computation, and power.³
Companies need help with AI deployments and easing their workforces through the AI transition. Best practices and strategic partnerships can help. It starts with clarifying the challenges AI can solve.
Why AI And Why Now
Businesses typically look to AI to help them in two critical areas: business productivity and IT operations. AI can represent a game-changer, solving different challenges across an organization.
For workers, digital debt is a serious problem. Digital debt accrues when workers take in more information than they can process effectively while still doing justice to the rest of their jobs. It’s a fact that digital debt saps productivity, ultimately depressing the bottom line.
No wonder 68% of workers report not having enough time to get things done during the workday.4 Yet, pulling extra nighttime or early morning hours to try to get ahead is not a viable solution, it deprives them of sleep and time with family and fuels information overload. But AI productivity tools can help them handle more information in less time, freeing them up for more interesting and productive tasks without losing sleep.
Ransomware and other malware attacks keep expanding and hitting organizations hard. Threats against network infrastructure are also rising, driven by state-sponsored attackers.5 The most effective countermeasure: AI-enabled defense moving at machine speed and scale. Zero-trust frameworks are also critical for effective cyber defense.
IT organizations have long grappled with talent shortages. AI can augment IT pros’ efforts without putting impossible demands on their time as they provision devices, add users, manage policies, and perform other routine tasks. It can also help security analysts spot suspicious patterns in network traffic, automate defensive actions, and free up their time.
How AI Helps Key Sectors
In addition to helping business and IT users tackle common challenges, AI provides specialized benefits to individual industries.
- Manufacturing: AI improves quality control with machine vision and algorithms that detect production flaws sooner, reducing waste. By bringing sophisticated AI and compute technology to the point of use, front-line workers, engineers, and managers will leverage faster insights and more powerful, efficient devices. And AI offers opportunities for manufacturers to institutionalize “tribal” wisdom, codifying the experience of seasoned operators for newer recruits to access on the shop floor on demand.
- Healthcare: AI can get patients the care they need faster with intelligent chat agents. It provides support for clinicians, for example, through automated notetaking, freeing them up to spend more time with patients and less on paperwork. In the back office, it helps support staff with billing and other functions. Many more benefits will be realized as part of the AI-in-healthcare revolution.
- Retail: AI is reshaping both online and brick-and-mortar operations. AI chat enhances the customer experience for shopping and support, delivering personalized recommendations and streamlining returns. In-store, machine vision, and AI analyze traffic patterns to help marketers optimize product placement and prevent losses. Retailers using AI also benefit from increased margins thanks to optimized inventory management and pricing strategies based on real-time data.
Realizing these capabilities and benefits requires good planning and purposeful coordination of many moving parts, from network infrastructure to effective data governance practices and people management.
Putting The Pieces Together
As noted in our AI strategy eBook, a sample use case is a better starting point than going “all in” with AI and trying to boil the ocean. With a specific use case identified, leaders can make technology decisions based on an immediate, real-world need rather than chasing the latest shiny AI object.
When selecting a use case, look for potential productivity gains that have the potential to deliver a high return on investment relatively quickly. Customer service and marketing are two areas where companies can achieve quick wins for AI applications.
Preparing your people and organization for AI is critical to avoid unnecessary uncertainty. Any new technology requires adjustment. AI, with its wide range of capabilities, can be anxiety-provoking for people concerned about their jobs and the amount of work that will be asked of them. Leaders should engage their people on AI plans early and seek their input.
Finally, organizations will benefit from partnerships with AI experts who work closely with the major IT and AI vendors. Experts can help in-house professionals put all the pieces together for a powerful, cohesive AI strategy that delivers competitive advantages for the future.
